name: Cambodia
summary_text: Cambodia is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex activity or gender expression — and the government is formally cooperative: it accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations at its 2024 Universal Periodic Review, including legal gender recognition, and hosted the UN Independent Expert on SOGI in 2023. Phnom Penh and Siem Reap have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors. The risks are street-level and police-level rather than legal: the Cambodian Centre for Human Rights documents “shocking” harassment and abuse of transgender women in urban centres, including a reported Siem Reap police practice of targeting trans women (extortion and abuse). There is no legal gender recognition yet, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute. For a visitor: low probability of legal trouble; moderate probability of harassment if visibly trans outside tourist areas; police are a risk factor, not a protection, for trans women especially.

sources.title: Visit to Cambodia - Report of the Independent Expert on protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity | United Nations in Cambodia
sources.claim_summary: UN Independent Expert on SOGI Victor Madrigal-Borloz's report on his January 2023 visit to Cambodia: assesses implementation of standards on violence and discrimination based on SOGI, gives a panoramic view of the situation of LGBT and gender-diverse Cambodians, identifies good practices and challenges, and makes recommendations.

sources.title: Cambodia | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex activity, but Article 45 of the constitution defines marriage as between one husband and one wife; at its 2024 UPR Cambodia accepted all 12 LGBTIQ recommendations including seven toward marriage equality; no SOGISC discrimination protections; a 2018 two-men wedding ceremony in Kratie was interrupted by authorities.

sources.title: Abuses prevalent for Cambodia's transgender women: study - Phnom Penh Post
sources.claim_summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Phnom Penh Post article covers a study finding abuses prevalent against Cambodia's transgender women.

Rainbow Community Kampuchea (RoCK) page on Cambodia's 4th-cycle UPR: Cambodia officially accepted all 12 SOGIESC/LGBT+ recommendations in 2024 - marriage equality progress, legal gender recognition for self-defined identity, and anti-discrimination measures; includes the civil-society joint submission (Dec 2023) and summary factsheets.

UNDP/USAID 'Being LGBT in Asia: Cambodia Country Report' (2014): participatory review of the legal and social environment - the Civil Code's implicit non-recognition of same-sex marriage, varying police interpretations of laws, Buddhist perceptions of sexuality, and cultural attitudes.
Frommer's travel guide: 'Tips for Gay and Lesbian Travelers' in Cambodia - practical travel advice for LGBT visitors (page largely navigation content at fetch time).

sources.title: 8 in 10 Cambodian queer women and trans men emotionally abused by family
sources.claim_summary: PinkNews (July 2019): RoCK study - 81% of young queer women and trans men in Cambodia suffer emotional abuse by family; violence includes disownment, beatings, forced marriages and forced rehab 'to fix his gender'; 35% of under-35s had considered suicide due to family rejection.
